title: Loosen an M10 nylon-insert locknut with an adjustable wrench: roll the jaw snug onto the flats, then turn
instruction: Roll the adjustable wrench's thumbwheel until its jaw is snug on the nut's flats, loosen the nut at least 60 degrees counterclockwise with it, and let go of the wrench.
context: An adjustable wrench has to be sized to the nut before it is used: its knurled thumbwheel is rolled with a fingertip until the jaw closes on the flats. A jaw left wider than the nut's corners swings round it; a jaw left loose turns a light nut but bears on its corners, which rounds them or slips under load. General maintenance and repair workers (O*NET 49-9071.00, about 1.5 million in the US, BLS OEWS), electricians (about 0.8 million) and automotive technicians (about 0.7 million) set and use adjustable wrenches every day, among them on nylon-insert locknuts (DIN 985) that resist turning all the way off. Here the jaw starts open 23 mm round an M10 locknut: a fingertip rolls the thumbwheel about two turns until the jaw is snug, then the nut is turned one flat against its nylon insert, and the wrench is let go on the loosened nut.
setup: Station bench; positions in m from the midpoint between the arm bases (left y +0.305, right y -0.305), x away from the arms, z up. Both arms at ready. One fixed layout (object_jitter 0); nothing depends on the seed. A painted 330 x 340 x 8 mm steel plate centred at (0.250, -0.050) holds an ISO 4017 M10 x 25 screw (8.8) standing up through a tapped hole at (0.280, 0.060), 17 mm above the plate. On the plate round the screw: a DIN 9021 M10 washer (30 x 2.5 mm), and on it a DIN 985 M10 nylon-insert locknut (steel 8, zinc plated, 17 mm across flats) run down with a wrench until it touches the washer, not tightened, with a paint mark across its top and the washer. A Bahco 8071 adjustable wrench (205 mm, 255 g), its jaw set to 23 mm on its scale, lies round the nut with its fixed jaw flat against one flat and the nut against the throat: head on the washer, handle pointing back and to the right (150 deg from +x), its end on the plate.
scoring: Whole-trial 0 if the nut is turned clockwise (tightened) past 10 deg (paint mark, trial video). At the end: 1.0 if the nut is loosened at least 60 deg counterclockwise (one flat past its paint mark), the jaw reads at most 17.5 mm on the wrench's scale (a 0.5 mm feeler leaf beside it must not pass between a jaw and its flat), the wrench lies flat (within 15 deg) on the plate, both grippers are at least 30 mm from wrench and nut, and wrench and nut have stayed still for 1.0 s (trial video; 1 mm and 0.5 deg in the simulator). 0.5 if the nut is loosened 60 deg with the jaw at most 17.5 mm but the rest is not met (a hand still on the wrench, the wrench held up or off the plate). 0.25 if the jaw is at most 17.5 mm with the nut turned less than 60 deg, or the nut is loosened 60 deg with the jaw over 17.5 mm at the end or as the turn began (read as the nut first passes 10 deg; on the video, with the head covered, a loose pull shows as a free swing of the handle before the paint mark moves: 12.4 deg at 18.4 mm against 3.7 at 17.5 mm). 0 otherwise (an open jaw swings round the nut).
run_limit: 1,800 steps (90 s at 20 Hz): the reference run takes 49.5 s; the rest is room for a learned policy
reset_notes: Turn the nut clockwise with the wrench until it just touches the washer (do not tighten), line its paint mark up with the washer's, set the jaw to 23 mm on the wrench's scale, and lay the wrench round the nut at 150 deg from +x as in the start photo, its fixed jaw flat against one flat (head on the washer, handle end on the plate). About 40 s.
fidelity: The task stops at the loosened nut: the simulator cannot slide a snug jaw off the hex without dragging it, so the wrench stays on the nut, as a person pausing before the next turn would. Nut on a hinge against 1.5 N m (ISO 2320), turned only through the jaws. Stand-ins: knurl 0.5 mm proud of the head; nut 0.25 kg, jaw 80 g; jaw friction 1.0 (dry steel 0.2).
